opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's really important, and I try to keep those relationships as good as possible. I know most of the leaders of the major labs quite well; many of us have known each other for over a decade, some since well before AI was fashionable, when it was a fairly niche academic pursuit. So there's a lot of shared history there.

The way I think about it is that we're all, in a sense, stewards of something that's going to be one of the most transformative technologies in human history. That's a huge responsibility, and it goes beyond any single company's commercial interests. There's obviously intense competition right now, and that's natural; it drives progress and pushes everyone to do better work. But underneath the competition, I think it's critical that we maintain lines of communication and a degree of mutual respect, because as we get closer to AGI, there are going to be moments where coordination really matters: on safety standards, on how we deploy the most capable systems, on making sure we don't end up in a race to the bottom where people cut corners.

So I try to stay in touch, talk regularly when I can, and keep things collegial even when the press or the broader narrative makes it look like a cutthroat fight. I've always believed the scientific method and a scientific mindset should guide how we approach this, and science at its best is collaborative. It's built on sharing ideas, peer review, building on each other's work.

I'd also say it's not just the lab leaders. It's about building trust with governments, academia, and civil society too, because ultimately getting this right is going to require a kind of international cooperation. My hope is that the relationships we build now, while the stakes are still manageable, become the foundation for the harder conversations we'll need to have in the coming years.

r001.rationale: The response says lab leaders should maintain lines of communication and stay in touch, explaining that coordination matters for safety standards and deployment of capable systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to say first that I know most of these people, and in many cases I've known them for a very long time. Some of them I've known since before any of this was a big deal, when it was a few hundred people at NeurIPS and we'd all be in the same hallway arguing about whether deep learning was going anywhere. So there's a kind of shared history there that I think matters.

And I try to keep those relationships going, really quite deliberately. I'll have dinner with people, I'll see them at conferences, we'll have calls sometimes. Because fundamentally, I think we're all working on the same problem. We may have different views about how to get there, different views on timelines, different views on the right way to structure the organisations doing it, and sometimes those disagreements are pretty sharp. But on the thing that actually matters, which is that this technology is going to be the most consequential thing humanity has ever built and we need to get it right, I think there's more agreement than the public sometimes sees.

The way I think about it is that competition is good for the science. It pushes everyone, it means things move fast, it means ideas get tested. And I'm quite competitive myself, I've always been, from chess onwards. So I don't pretend otherwise. But there's a difference between competing hard on the research and the products, and competing in a way that corrodes the ability to coordinate when coordination is needed. And it will be needed. If we get close to systems that are genuinely powerful, there are going to be moments where the labs need to talk to each other honestly about what they're seeing, about safety evaluations, about what thresholds mean, and you can't build that trust in the moment. It has to already exist.

So I treat it a bit like, you know, a tough but respectful rivalry. You want the other side to be strong, actually. You want to be able to pick up the phone. And I think most of the people leading these efforts, whatever their public positioning, would say something similar if you asked them privately. The thing I worry about more is the pressure the whole system is under, the commercial pressure, the geopolitical pressure, which can make it harder for individuals to act on those relationships even when they want to. That's the bit I try to protect, as much as I can.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions calls and being able to pick up the phone, and says leaders need to talk honestly about safety evaluations and coordinate when powerful systems emerge.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish competition from personal relationships. You can compete very hard on the science and on building useful products, while still respecting the people doing the work elsewhere and keeping a dialogue open.

And with AI, there’s an additional responsibility. Some of the questions we’re facing—particularly around safety and how these systems are deployed—affect everybody. We need to be able to talk frankly about those things, even when we disagree or have competing commercial interests.

That doesn’t mean sharing everything. There are legitimate boundaries. But I think you want enough trust that, if something concerning happens, you can pick up the phone and have a serious conversation. That trust is much easier to build before you need it.

r001.rationale: The response says competing lab leaders should keep dialogue open and talk frankly about AI safety, with enough trust to call one another if something concerning happens. This identifies communication as a way to address shared safety concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the competition from the bigger mission. Of course, we’re competing to build the best systems, and that can be very intense. But we’re also working on a technology that could have profound consequences for everyone. So I think it’s important to keep those relationships constructive and the channels of communication open, particularly around safety.

You can disagree with someone’s approach and still respect them. Ideally, you want enough trust that you can pick up the phone and have an honest conversation when something really matters. Competition can drive progress, but it shouldn’t prevent cooperation on the things we all need to get right.

r001.rationale: It says leaders should keep communication channels open, particularly around safety, and describes cooperation on shared priorities despite competition.
